claims.text: The target alloy is equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
As-cast equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi is a homogeneous, single-phase solid solution with a uniform atomic distribution.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi alloy contains minimal nanoscale ordering or precipitates.
The relatively low hardness and strength of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi result from its lack of nanoscale dislocation obstacles.
Precipitates or chemically ordered regions can act as obstacles or pinning sites for dislocations.
In simple solid-solution CoCrFeNiTi, plastic deformation occurs mainly by dislocation glide with minimal interruption.
Relatively unhindered dislocation glide gives CoCrFeNiTi favorable plasticity.
Relatively unhindered dislocation glide gives CoCrFeNiTi favorable machinability.
Heat treatment or a minor compositional adjustment can induce nanoscale ordering or precipitation in CoCrFeNiTi.
Induced nanoscale ordering or precipitates would increase barriers to dislocation motion.
CoCrFeNiTi samples containing induced nanoscale ordering or precipitates should have higher yield strength than the homogeneous starting state.
CoCrFeNiTi samples containing induced nanoscale ordering or precipitates should have higher hardness than the homogeneous starting state.
The strengthened samples may exhibit a slight reduction in ductility.
The hypothesis is intended to apply from room temperature to approximately 600 °C under quasi-static indentation, micropillar compression, tensile, or compression loading.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the alloy remains a single-phase solid solution.
If coarse or secondary phases are introduced, strengthening mechanisms other than the proposed nanoscale-obstacle mechanism may dominate.

contradictions.description: The intervention explicitly proposes forming precipitates, while the boundary says the mechanism is expected to hold only if the alloy remains a single-phase solid solution and treats secondary phases as invoking other mechanisms. Precipitates ordinarily constitute a second phase, so the precipitate branch conflicts with the stated boundary unless coherent nanoscale ordering within one phase is considered separately.
